why_how.text: Traffic signals keep intersections flowing, and each light and arrow has a precise meaning.
Knowing what to do when a signal fails or an officer takes over prevents confusion at busy corners.

scenario.text: During a storm, Ana reaches an intersection where the traffic lights are completely dark.

reasoning.text: A signal with no power is treated as if it were a stop sign.

result.text: Ana stops fully, takes her turn, and proceeds when the way is clear.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a dark traffic signal like a green light or a yield sign.

correction.text: A light that is out or malfunctioning is handled like a stop sign.

memory_support.text: Steady red waits; flashing red stops then goes.

prompt.text: You stop at a flashing red light and the cross street is empty. What may you do next?

answer.text: Go, since the way is clear after your full stop.

rationale.text: A flashing red means stop and then go when safe, while a steady red means wait for green.

narration.text: Welcome to the chapter on signals, pavement markings and lane controls. Traffic signals are lights that tell you when and where to stop or go, and they keep traffic flowing at busy intersections. This first lesson covers how signals are arranged, what you will find at many country intersections, what to do when a light loses power or when an officer is directing traffic, and then the four kinds of red signal: steady red, flashing red, steady red arrow and flashing red arrow. Each one requires a stop, but they differ in what happens after it.

lines.text: Red top, yellow middle, green bottom.

narration.text: Traffic signals are usually at intersections, and the lights are arranged with red on top, yellow in the middle and green at the bottom. Knowing the order lets you tell at a glance which light is lit. A lot of intersections out in the country have only a single yellow or red light instead of a full set. Read a single light by its color and by whether it is steady or flashing, using the rules in this lesson and the next, and approach carefully. Whatever the setup, the color and whether it is steady or flashing tell you what to do, and the rest of this lesson explains each red signal in turn.

lines.text: No power or not working: a stop sign.

narration.text: If a traffic light loses power or is not working properly, proceed as if the signal were a stop sign. Every driver stops, and drivers take turns just as they would at a four-way stop. If you see a police officer directing traffic at a signal, follow the officer's directions, even if they differ from what the light shows. Be ready for hand signals as you approach. In both situations, slow down early and watch the other drivers closely, because not everyone will react the same way. Patience and a full stop keep these intersections safe for everyone.

lines.text: Steady red: stop, wait for green.
Flashing red: stop, then go when safe.

narration.text: At a steady red light, come to a full stop. You must wait until the light turns green and there is no cross traffic before going. At a flashing red light, you must also come to a full stop, but then you may go when it is safe to do so. So the stop is the same; the difference is what releases you. A steady red releases you only when it turns green. A flashing red releases you as soon as the way is clear, much like a stop sign. Look carefully at the light to see whether it is steady or flashing before you decide. Keep the two apart.

lines.text: Steady red arrow: stop, wait for green.
Flashing red arrow: stop, then go when safe.

narration.text: Red arrows control turns and follow the same pattern as red lights. At a steady red arrow, you must come to a full stop and wait for the light to turn green before turning. At a flashing red arrow, you must come to a full stop, and you may then turn when it is safe to do so. Always check which lane an arrow is over before deciding whether it applies to you. So a red arrow is read exactly like a red light: the word steady means wait for green, and the word flashing means stop and then go when the way is clear. Treat the arrow as a rule for your turn, and do not start turning just because the drivers going straight have a different signal.

Here is the trap. Because both steady and flashing red require a full stop, people forget the difference afterward. Both a steady red and a flashing red require a full stop, but after a flashing red you may go once it is safe, while after a steady red you wait for green. Arrows work the same way: a steady red arrow means stop and wait for green, while a flashing red arrow means stop and then go when safe. When a question describes a red signal, look for the word steady or flashing first, because that word decides the answer.

Here is a quick check: you stop at a flashing red light and the cross street is empty. What may you do next? Think about what releases you from each kind of red. You may go, since the way is clear after your full stop. A flashing red means stop and then go when safe, while a steady red means wait for green. If the light were steady red instead, you would have to stay stopped until it turned green and cross traffic cleared, even with no one around. And a completely dark signal would be treated as a stop sign. Each red has its own release.

lines.text: Dark signal: stop sign; officer: obey.
Steady waits; flashing goes when safe.

narration.text: To wrap up: signals stack red, yellow and green from top to bottom, and many country intersections have a single yellow or red light. Treat a dark or malfunctioning signal as a stop sign, and follow a police officer who is directing traffic. At a steady red, stop and wait for green and for cross traffic to clear; at a flashing red, stop and then go when safe. Red arrows match: a steady red arrow waits for green, a flashing red arrow lets you turn after stopping when safe. Next you will learn when you may turn on a red light.

why_how.text: Turning on red saves time, but only when it is legal and safe.
A fixed sequence of stopping and yielding makes every turn on red safe.

scenario.text: At a red light on a two-way street, Jay wants to turn left onto a one-way street.

reasoning.text: A left on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street.

result.text: Jay waits for the green light before turning left.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a left turn on red is allowed onto any one-way street.

correction.text: Both streets must be one-way: left on red is allowed only from a one-way onto a one-way.

memory_support.text: Right on red if allowed; left only one-way to one-way.

prompt.text: You are on a one-way street at a red light and want to turn left onto another one-way street. What must you do first?

answer.text: Come to a full stop and yield to all traffic before turning.

rationale.text: Left on red is allowed from a one-way onto a one-way, but every turn on red starts with a full stop and a yield.

lines.text: When right on red is allowed.

narration.text: This short lesson covers turning on a red light. Wisconsin allows some turns on red, but each has conditions, and the conditions for right turns and left turns are very different. You will learn when a right turn on red is allowed, the one narrow case where a left turn on red is allowed, and the sequence every turn on red must follow, whichever direction you are turning. These rules are a favorite on knowledge tests because the left-turn rule is so specific, so pay close attention to the exact wording in this lesson. Read every word of each rule.

lines.text: Right on red: safe and no sign against it.
Left on red: one-way onto one-way only.

narration.text: You can turn right on red if it is safe to do so and there is no sign prohibiting it. Look for a No Turn on Red sign before you start, because some intersections forbid it. A left turn on red is much more limited: you may turn left on red only if you are turning from a one-way street onto a one-way street. If either street carries two-way traffic, a left on red is not allowed, and you wait for the green. So right on red is the common case, while left on red applies only where both streets are one-way. When in doubt, wait for the green.

When turning on red, you need to stop first, yield to all traffic, and then proceed, staying in your lane. The full stop comes first even when the road looks clear; rolling through a red light to turn is not allowed. Yield means letting cross traffic and pedestrians go before you, including people in the crosswalk you will turn across. Staying in your lane means turning into the nearest lane of the new road rather than swinging wide into a far lane. This sequence applies to both right turns and the allowed left turns on red.

lines.text: Right: whenever safe and not forbidden.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Learners who know right on red is usually allowed assume left on red works the same way. Right turns on red are allowed whenever safe and not forbidden by a sign, but left turns on red are allowed only from a one-way street onto a one-way street. A question may describe a driver on a two-way street wanting to turn left onto a one-way street; that turn is not allowed on red. Check both streets before deciding: the street you are on and the street you are turning onto must both be one-way. Both streets must be one-way.

Here is a quick check: you are on a one-way street at a red light and want to turn left onto another one-way street. What must you do first? Think about the sequence for every turn on red. You come to a full stop and yield to all traffic before turning. Left on red is allowed from a one-way onto a one-way, but every turn on red starts with a full stop and a yield, then you proceed staying in your lane. If either street were two-way, you would wait for the green light instead. The stop and the yield always come first, whatever the direction of the turn.

lines.text: Left on red: one-way to one-way.

narration.text: In summary: you may turn right on red when it is safe and no sign prohibits it. You may turn left on red only when turning from a one-way street onto another one-way street. Whichever way you turn, stop first, yield to all traffic, and then proceed while staying in your lane. If you are unsure whether both streets are one-way, wait for the green light. Next you will learn the yellow and green signals, which have their own steady and flashing versions and their own traps about turning left and yielding. Careful turns on red keep the intersection safe.

why_how.text: Yellow signals warn of change, and knowing them prevents both red-light running and sudden stops.
Green signals give permission, but they do not cancel your duty to yield.

scenario.text: Ben is halfway through an intersection when his light turns yellow and he brakes hard.

reasoning.text: If you are already in the intersection when the yellow comes on, do not stop; continue through.

result.text: Ben keeps going and clears the intersection.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a steady green light means you may turn left without yielding.

correction.text: On a steady green you may turn left only when it is safe, because oncoming traffic has the right-of-way.

memory_support.text: Steady yellow stop; flashing yellow caution.

prompt.text: You see a flashing yellow arrow for your left turn. What must you do?

answer.text: Yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians first, then turn with caution.

rationale.text: A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn after yielding, while a steady yellow arrow warns the arrow is about to turn red.

narration.text: This lesson covers yellow and green signals. Yellow signals warn that something is about to change or that you must take extra care, and each has a steady and a flashing version with different meanings. Green signals give you permission to go, but they never remove your duty to yield to others the law protects. You will learn the steady yellow light, what to do if it appears while you are already in the intersection, the flashing yellow light, both yellow arrows, the steady green light, left turns on green, and the green arrow.

lines.text: Stop before entering if you can.

narration.text: A steady yellow light means the light is about to change to red. You must slow down and stop before entering the intersection. If you are already in the intersection when the yellow light comes on, do not stop; you can continue through the intersection. Stopping in the middle would leave you blocking cross traffic when their light turns green. So the decision point is the edge of the intersection: if you have not reached it and can stop safely, stop; if you are already past it, finish crossing smoothly without speeding up sharply.

lines.text: Steady yellow arrow: red is coming.
Flashing yellow arrow: yield, then turn.

narration.text: A flashing yellow light means slow down, check for cross traffic and proceed with caution. You do not have to stop, but be ready to. Yellow arrows control turns. A steady yellow arrow means the arrow is about to change to red, and you should stop if it is safe to do so. A flashing yellow arrow means you may turn, but you must yield first before turning and proceed with caution, letting oncoming traffic and pedestrians go before you. Never treat a flashing yellow arrow as a green arrow, because other traffic can still be coming toward you.

lines.text: Go through, but still yield as required.
Stopped? Let cross traffic clear first.
Left on green: oncoming has the right-of-way.

narration.text: A steady green light means you can go through the intersection, but you must still yield to emergency vehicles and others as required by law. If you are stopped and the light turns green, you must allow cross traffic to clear before you go ahead, because some drivers may still be finishing their crossing. If you are turning left, a steady green light means you may turn, but only when it is safe to do so; oncoming traffic has the right-of-way. Wait in the intersection for a safe gap, then complete the turn. A green light means go when it is safe.

lines.text: No oncoming or crossing traffic should move.

narration.text: A steady green arrow means you can turn in the direction of the arrow. There should be no oncoming or crossing traffic while the arrow is green, so the turn is protected from oncoming traffic. Even so, remember to watch for pedestrians, who may still be in the crosswalk, and for drivers who ignore their red light. Even on a green arrow you still watch for pedestrians, and even on a steady green you still yield to emergency vehicles. A green signal is permission to go when safe, never a promise that no one else is in the way.

lines.text: Green ball: left turn yields to oncoming.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Both a steady green ball and a green arrow let you turn left, so learners treat them the same. On a steady green ball, a left turn must yield to oncoming traffic, while under a green arrow no oncoming or crossing traffic should be moving. A third signal adds to the confusion: the flashing yellow arrow, which also lets you turn but only after yielding. When a question asks whether you must yield on a left turn, look at the signal: green ball or flashing yellow arrow means yield; green arrow means protected, but still watch for pedestrians.

Here is a quick check: you see a flashing yellow arrow for your left turn. What must you do? Recall the two yellow arrows. You yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians first, then turn with caution. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn after yielding, while a steady yellow arrow warns that the arrow is about to turn red, so you should stop if you safely can. If the arrow changes to steady green, your turn becomes protected, though you would still watch for pedestrians in the crosswalk before you go. Yield first, every time.

lines.text: Steady yellow: stop unless already in.

narration.text: In summary: a steady yellow means red is coming, so stop before the intersection unless you are already in it. A flashing yellow means slow, check cross traffic and proceed with caution. A steady yellow arrow warns of red; a flashing yellow arrow means yield, then turn. A steady green lets you go, but you still yield to emergency vehicles, let cross traffic clear after stopping, and yield to oncoming traffic on a left turn. A steady green arrow is a protected turn, but you still watch for pedestrians. Next come the white pavement lines and crosswalks.

why_how.text: Pavement lines tell you where you may drive, pass and turn, even where no sign is posted.
Crosswalk lines show where to stop so pedestrians can cross safely.

scenario.text: Kai is in the left of two lanes going his way, separated by a solid white line, and wants to move right to avoid a stalled car.

reasoning.text: A solid white line between lanes may be crossed to avoid a hazard or to turn within the next block.

result.text: Kai checks his mirror and blind spot and moves right around the stalled car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a solid white line between lanes may be crossed whenever it is safe.

correction.text: Only a dashed white line may be crossed whenever it is safe; a solid white line only for a hazard or a turn within the next block.

memory_support.text: Dashed white, cross when safe; solid white, stay.

prompt.text: You stop at a crosswalk with a solid white line. Where should your front wheels be?

answer.text: Just before the solid white line, not on the crosswalk.

rationale.text: Your front wheels stop just short of the solid white line, and you never stop on the crosswalk itself.

narration.text: This lesson begins the pavement markings part of the chapter. Lines and symbols painted on the road divide it into lanes and carry rules even where there are no signs. You will learn what pavement markings do in general, what the white and yellow edge lines tell you, how dashed and solid white lines between lanes differ, and how white arrows guide you. Then the lesson covers crosswalks: where they are, where to stop, and why you never stop on one. The next lesson turns to yellow lines and the rules for passing. Lines are rules painted on the road.

Line markings and symbols on the roadway divide it into lanes. They tell you when you can pass or change lanes and which lanes you can use for turns. Line colors also tell you whether you are on a one-way or two-way roadway: white lines separate traffic going the same direction, while yellow lines are tied to traffic going the other way. Learning to read them quickly lets you understand an unfamiliar road at a glance. White and yellow lines each have their own job, so the color is the first clue whenever you look down at the pavement. A quick glance at the lines can tell you whether you may pass, whether your lane turns, and which direction traffic flows beside you.

lines.text: Solid white: right edge of the lane.
Yellow: left edge of lanes going your way.

narration.text: Edge and lane lines frame where you drive. A solid white line indicates the right edge of the traffic lane. A solid or dashed yellow line indicates the left edge of the traffic lanes going in your direction. So on a normal road, you have white on your right and yellow on your left. If you ever find yellow on your right, you are likely facing the wrong way, for example on a one-way street or an exit ramp, so stop and check. White lines separate lanes going the same way, while the yellow line marks the left edge of the lanes going your way.

lines.text: Solid white: hazard or turn only.

narration.text: White dashed lines divide lanes of traffic going in the same direction, and you can cross them when it is safe. A white arrow on the pavement shows what direction that lane needs to go, such as turn only or straight only. A solid white line between lanes means you cannot cross. You can only cross it if there is a hazard or you are turning within the next block. Plan your lane well before you reach a solid white line, so you do not need to cross it. In short, dashed white lines invite safe lane changes, while solid white lines ask you to stay where you are unless a hazard or a turn just ahead makes crossing necessary.

lines.text: Stop just before the solid white line.

narration.text: A crosswalk is for pedestrians to walk safely across the intersection, and pedestrians may be given signals for when they can safely cross. When you stop, your front wheels should stop just before the solid white line. Do not stop on the crosswalk, because that forces people to walk around your car into traffic. Crosswalks are normally at intersections but can sometimes be in the middle of a street or block, so watch for crosswalk lines and pedestrian signs between intersections too, and be ready to stop for someone crossing there.

lines.text: Solid white: only a hazard or a turn.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Both lines are white and both separate lanes going the same way, so learners treat them alike. A white dashed line may be crossed when safe, while a solid white line between lanes may be crossed only for a hazard or a turn within the next block. And a solid white line across your lane at a crosswalk is a stop line, not a lane line. When a question describes a white line, ask two things: is it dashed or solid, and does it run along the lane or across it? Those two answers tell you what you may do. Direction and pattern decide.

lines.text: Crosswalk ahead: where do wheels stop?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you stop at a crosswalk marked with a solid white line. Where should your front wheels be? Picture the line across your lane. They should be just before the solid white line, not on the crosswalk. Your front wheels stop just short of the line, and you never stop on the crosswalk itself, so pedestrians have the whole space to cross. Remember that crosswalks can also be in the middle of a block, so the same stopping rule applies there, and pedestrians may have their own signals telling them when to walk.

lines.text: Dashed white crossable; solid white not.

narration.text: To wrap up: pavement lines divide the road into lanes, show where you may pass, change lanes and turn, and their color tells you one-way from two-way. A solid white line marks the right edge of your lane, and a solid or dashed yellow line marks the left edge of lanes going your way. Cross a white dashed line when safe; cross a solid white line between lanes only for a hazard or a turn within the next block. Stop with your front wheels just before a crosswalk's solid white line, never on the crosswalk. Next come yellow lines and passing.

why_how.text: Yellow lines separate you from oncoming traffic, so they decide where passing is safe and legal.
The exceptions to the no-passing lines are narrow, so knowing them exactly prevents dangerous passes.

scenario.text: Lily follows a tractor going well under half the speed limit on a road with double solid yellow lines.

reasoning.text: Passing a vehicle under half the limit is an exception, but it never applies to farm equipment.

result.text: Lily stays behind the tractor until the lines allow passing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a very slow tractor may be passed across a double yellow line.

correction.text: The slow-vehicle exception never applies to farm equipment.

memory_support.text: Dashed may, solid may not; your side decides.

prompt.text: Your side of the center has a solid yellow line, and the other side has a dashed line. May you pass?

answer.text: No. Only drivers on the dashed side may pass.

rationale.text: With mixed lines, the line nearest you decides: dashed on your side allows passing, solid on your side does not.

narration.text: This lesson covers the yellow lines that separate you from oncoming traffic and the rules they set for passing. You will learn what solid and double solid yellow lines mean, the two narrow exceptions that let you cross a double yellow line, what a dashed yellow line allows, how to read a dashed line beside a solid line, and the signs that sometimes mark passing zones. Passing on a two-lane road puts you in the path of oncoming traffic, so these rules are among the most important in the handbook. Patience on two-lane roads saves lives.

lines.text: Two solid lines: no passing either way.

narration.text: Solid yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. Two solid yellow lines mean that no lane of travel can pass; drivers in both directions must stay on their own side. When you see a double solid yellow line, stay in your lane and be patient, even behind a slower vehicle, until the markings change to allow passing again. Treat a double yellow line as a wall down the middle of the road. The only times you may cross it are the two narrow exceptions in the next slide, and even then only when it is safe. Passing anyway, even when the road ahead looks empty, is not allowed and puts you in the path of oncoming drivers.

lines.text: Turning into a driveway when safe.
Passing a vehicle under half the limit.

narration.text: There are two exceptions to the double yellow rule. You can cross the line if you turn into a driveway and it is safe to do so. You can also pass a vehicle going less than half the speed limit if it is safe, except if it is farm equipment. So a car crawling along far below the limit may be passed carefully, but a tractor or other farm machine may not be passed across a double yellow line, no matter how slowly it is moving. In both exceptions, the word safe matters: you still need a clear view and enough room. Both exceptions still require a clear view.

lines.text: Dashed beside solid: dashed side only.

narration.text: A dashed yellow line means you may pass other vehicles when it is safe to do so; watch for other traffic if you choose to pass. When a dashed yellow line runs beside a solid yellow line, you may pass if you are on the dashed side of the line, but if you are on the solid side, you may not pass. Some passing zones also have signs that tell you where you can and cannot pass. Whenever you consider a pass, look at the line closest to you first, then check that oncoming traffic is far enough away and that you will have room to return before the solid line resumes. If the signs say no passing, stay in your lane.

lines.text: Dashed on your side: may pass.
Solid on your side: may not.

narration.text: Here is the trap. With a dashed line beside a solid yellow line, drivers sometimes look at the wrong line. The line nearest you decides: dashed on your side allows passing, solid on your side does not. Another trap hides in the exceptions. The double yellow exceptions are turning into a driveway and passing a vehicle going under half the speed limit, and the second never applies to farm equipment. And remember the simple pair: a single dashed yellow line allows passing when safe, while two solid yellow lines forbid passing from either side.

lines.text: Solid on your side, dashed beyond?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on your side of the center there is a solid yellow line, and on the other side there is a dashed line. May you pass? Look at the line nearest you. The answer is no. Only drivers on the dashed side may pass. With mixed lines, the line nearest you decides: dashed on your side allows passing, solid on your side does not. Drivers coming the other way, who have the dashed line on their side, may pass when safe, which is one more reason to stay in your lane and watch ahead. Your side's line always decides.

lines.text: Exceptions: driveway, very slow non-farm vehicle.

narration.text: In summary: solid yellow lines separate opposite directions, and two solid yellow lines mean no one may pass. You may cross a double yellow line to turn into a driveway when safe, or to pass a vehicle going less than half the speed limit when safe, but never farm equipment. A dashed yellow line allows passing when safe. With a dashed line beside a solid one, only the dashed side may pass, and some zones also have signs marking where passing is allowed. Next you will learn the special lanes, starting with shared center and reversible lanes.

why_how.text: Special lanes let roads handle turning traffic and rush hours, but each has strict rules.
Overhead lights tell you which reversible lanes you may use at any moment.

scenario.text: Omar uses the shared center lane to pass a slow car on a busy street.

reasoning.text: A shared center lane is only for vehicles turning left or making a U-turn.

result.text: Omar stays in his lane and uses the center lane only when he turns left.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a shared center lane may be used for passing.

correction.text: A shared center lane is only for left turns and U-turns, from either direction.

memory_support.text: Red X closed, green arrow open, yellow X leave.

prompt.text: You are driving in a reversible lane and the light above it changes to a yellow X. What should you do?

answer.text: Move to a lane with a green arrow.

rationale.text: A yellow X means the lane is changing, a red X means closed, and a green arrow means open.

narration.text: Wisconsin has several special lanes, and the handbook says it is important to practice driving in them. This lesson covers two of them. The shared center lane runs down the middle of some roads and is used for turning. Reversible lanes change direction at different times of day and are controlled by special lights over each lane. Both are marked with yellow lines, but in different patterns, which is a common source of confusion. The next lesson covers reserved lanes and flex lanes, the remaining special lanes in the chapter.

lines.text: Only for left turns and U-turns.

narration.text: A shared center lane is only for vehicles turning left or making a U-turn. Vehicles can use this lane going in either direction, and white left-turn symbols show which direction you can turn. The lane has a solid yellow line and a dashed line on each side. You can cross the solid line when you want to make the left turn or U-turn, but be sure you enter the lane only if it is safe to do so. Because drivers from both directions share it, enter close to where you plan to turn and watch for a driver coming toward you in the same lane.

Reversible lanes have different operational hours for each lane, so a lane may carry traffic one way in the morning and the other way in the evening. Each lane is marked with double dashed yellow lines, and special lights over the lanes tell you which lanes you can use. A red X means the lane is closed. A green arrow means the lane is open. A yellow X means the lane is changing, so move to a lane with a green arrow. Because the directions change, always read the lights above every lane you use, instead of trusting the pattern you saw last time.

lines.text: Shared center: solid and dashed, turns only.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Both special lanes use yellow lines down the middle, so drivers mix them up. A shared center lane is marked with solid and dashed yellow lines and is used only for left turns and U-turns, while a reversible lane is marked with double dashed yellow lines and has different operating hours for each lane. Driving straight in a shared center lane is not allowed, and driving in a reversible lane under a red X is not allowed either. Read the line pattern and look up for lane lights to know which kind of lane you are in.

Here is a quick check: you are driving in a reversible lane and the light above it changes to a yellow X. What should you do? Recall the three lane lights. You move to a lane with a green arrow. A yellow X means the lane is changing, a red X means it is closed, and a green arrow means it is open. Do not wait until the light turns red to move over; the yellow X is your signal to change lanes safely now, using your mirrors, your signal and a check of your blind spot before you move. Act on the yellow X right away. Read the lights above every lane.

To sum up: a shared center lane is only for left turns and U-turns, can be used by traffic from either direction, and is marked with white left-turn arrows and solid and dashed yellow lines; cross the solid line into it only to turn, and only when safe. Reversible lanes run different hours for each lane, are marked with double dashed yellow lines, and use overhead lights: a red X means closed, a green arrow means open, and a yellow X means changing, so move to a green arrow lane. Next come reserved lanes and flex lanes. Practice these lanes with care.

why_how.text: Reserved lanes keep buses, bikes and car pools moving, so other drivers must stay out except to turn.
Flex lanes add space on busy highways, but only when the signs and lights say so.

scenario.text: Mia needs to turn right at a corner a full block ahead, and a bus lane runs along the curb.

reasoning.text: You may drive in a reserved lane only to turn across it within the next half of a block.

result.text: Mia stays out of the bus lane until she is within half a block of her turn.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any vehicle may use an open flex lane.

correction.text: Large trucks may never use a flex lane, even when its green arrow is lit.

memory_support.text: Reserved lane: half a block to turn; flex lane: no trucks.

prompt.text: You are in a flex lane and the light ahead changes to a yellow X. What must you do?

rationale.text: A yellow X means the flex lane is closing so you merge out, while a red X means it is already closed.

lines.text: Lanes for buses, bikes and car pools.

narration.text: This final lesson of the chapter covers two more special lanes. Reserved lanes are set aside for particular vehicles such as buses, bikes or car pools, and you need to know when other drivers may enter them. Flex lanes are paved shoulders that certain highways open as travel lanes when traffic is heavy or during special events. Both depend on reading signs, pavement markings and lights carefully. You will learn the reserved lane rules, the colors and hours that may apply, and how flex lane lights and signs tell you when to use or leave the lane.

lines.text: White diamond on sign and pavement.

narration.text: Reserved lanes are for special vehicles only, and the signs often have a white diamond posted at the side of the sign and on the roadway. It is illegal to travel in one of these lanes unless you are operating that type of vehicle. You can travel in the lane if you need to turn across it in the next half of a block. If there is a bicyclist in the lane, move behind them and make your turn once it is safe to do so. Entering earlier than half a block before your turn, or using the lane to pass traffic, is not allowed. The half-block rule is the key.

title.text: Bus, bike and car pool lanes

lines.text: Some signs list days and hours.
Lanes may be painted red, green or gray.

narration.text: Some reserved lanes are only for buses, others only for bikes, and some for buses and car pools. Some signs show the hours and days you can drive in the lane, so a restriction may apply only at certain times. Bus or bike lanes might be painted in different colors, such as red, green or gray. Follow the markings in the street lettering and the posted signage. Because rules can vary by time and location, read each sign as you approach rather than assuming that a lane you used freely on Sunday is open to you on a Monday morning.

lines.text: Shoulder used as a travel lane.

narration.text: Some highways allow you to use the paved shoulder as a travel lane, and signage tells you when you can use it as a flex lane. A solid yellow line separates this special lane, and traffic volumes and special events dictate when it is open. No large trucks can drive in the flex lane. If there is an incident along the flex lane route, the yellow and red X's will tell drivers to merge into the next lane. A Merge sign marks the end of the flex lane, where you merge back into the general-purpose lanes, which are the normal lanes of the highway.

Flex lanes use lights much like reversible lanes. A green arrow means the lane is open and can be used. A yellow X means the lane is closing, so you need to merge to the general-purpose lanes. A red X means the lane is closed and cannot be used. A regulatory sign posted next to the flex lane signs gives general directions on how to use the lane. Watch the lights the whole time you are in a flex lane, not just when you enter it, because the lane can close ahead of you while you are driving in it. Keep watching the lights.

Here is the trap. When a flex lane shows a green arrow, drivers assume anyone may use it. A flex lane is the paved shoulder opened by signs as a travel lane, but large trucks may never use it even when its green arrow is lit. Reserved lanes work the same way: an empty bus lane is still reserved, and other vehicles may enter it only to turn across it within the next half of a block. In both cases, an open-looking lane is not an invitation; the signs and lights decide who may use it and when. Signs and lights decide every time.

lines.text: Yellow X ahead in a flex lane?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving in a flex lane and the light ahead changes to a yellow X. What must you do? Recall the three flex lane lights. You merge into the general-purpose lanes. A yellow X means the flex lane is closing, so you merge out, while a red X means it is already closed. Signal, check your mirrors and blind spot, and move over smoothly. If you see a Merge sign instead, that marks the planned end of the flex lane, and you merge back into the normal lanes there in the same careful way. Smooth merging keeps traffic safe.

lines.text: Reserved lanes: turn within half a block.
Flex lanes: lights decide; no trucks.

narration.text: To finish the chapter: reserved lanes are only for the vehicles named on the sign, often marked with a white diamond, and others may enter only to turn across them within the next half block, moving behind any bicyclist. Signs may list days and hours, and bus or bike lanes may be painted red, green or gray. Flex lanes are shoulders opened by signs, separated by a solid yellow line, and never used by large trucks. A green arrow means open, a yellow X means closing so merge out, a red X means closed, and a Merge sign marks the end.
